skill_title: Interpret profit and loss zones from a cost/revenue graph
notes: All fresh inline stimuli. Heavy emphasis on interpretation rather than pure calculation.

stimulus.inline:
**Bongi's Cake Bakery**
- Cost: R1 000 fixed + R20 per cake.
- Income: R45 per cake.
- Break-even: 40 cakes / R1 800.

items.question: Bongi makes and sells 30 cakes in March. State whether the business is in profit or loss and calculate the amount.

stimulus.inline: **Bongi's Cake Bakery** — break-even at 40 cakes / R1 800.

items.question: Bongi makes and sells 55 cakes in April. Calculate her profit.

stimulus.inline: **Bongi's Cake Bakery** — break-even at 40 cakes / R1 800.

items.question: Explain in your own words what the 'loss zone' on the cost/income graph represents for Bongi.
items.expectedAnswer: The loss zone is the part of the graph (below 40 cakes) where the cost line sits above the income line — every cake sold in this range produces some income but not enough to cover the fixed and variable costs, so Bongi loses money overall.
workingSteps: Identify the loss zone: x-values below break-even.
Describe the relative positions of the cost and income graphs in that zone.
Translate to business meaning: income inadequate to cover costs.

stimulus.inline: **Bongi's Cake Bakery** — break-even at 40 cakes.

items.question: Bongi forecasts she can sell 50 cakes a month. Demand then drops by 30%. What happens to the business?
items.expectedAnswer: 30% drop on 50 = 15 cakes lost, so new demand = 35 cakes. 35 is below the break-even point of 40, so Bongi moves from profit zone into loss zone and starts losing money each month.
workingSteps: State the business is now in loss zone.
Calculate loss: cost R1 700, income R1 575, loss R125 (optional).

stimulus.inline: **Sipho's Taxi** — break-even ≈ 715 km/month. Cost R5 000 fixed + R8/km. Revenue R15/km.

items.question: Sipho drives 900 km in a month. Calculate his profit.

stimulus.inline: **Sipho's Taxi** — break-even ≈ 715 km/month.

items.question: Sipho drives 500 km in a month. Is the business in profit or loss zone? Calculate the amount.

stimulus.inline: **Sipho's Taxi** — fuel price rises significantly, pushing his per-km cost from R8 to R11.

items.question: What happens to the break-even point and which zone is more 'reachable' (easier to fall into)?
items.expectedAnswer: Break-even quantity rises. New equation: R5 000 = (15 − 11)n = 4n → n = 1 250 km. The break-even km has jumped from 715 to 1 250, so Sipho now has to drive much further before reaching profit. The loss zone has become larger / 'more reachable'.
workingSteps: Interpret in business terms: bigger loss zone, profit harder to achieve.

stimulus.inline: **Lerato's T-shirt printing** — R3 000 fixed + R30/shirt. Sells for R80/shirt. Break-even: 60 shirts / R4 800.

items.question: Lerato sells 100 shirts in May. Calculate her profit.

stimulus.inline: **Lerato's T-shirt printing** — break-even at 60 shirts.

items.question: Lerato sells exactly 60 shirts in June. State her profit or loss.
workingSteps: Profit = 0. Loss = 0. Neither in profit nor loss zone.

stimulus.inline: **Lerato's T-shirt printing** — break-even 60, R3 000 fixed + R30/shirt, sell @ R80.

items.question: A friend tells Lerato that 'as long as you sell at least 1 shirt, you're making money'. Explain why this is wrong using the cost/income graph.
items.expectedAnswer: Income from 1 shirt is only R80, but the fixed cost is already R3 000 before any shirts are sold. The cost graph starts at R3 000 on the y-axis; the income graph starts at R0. Below the break-even of 60 shirts, the cost line sits above the income line, so Lerato loses money on every sale below that point. She must sell 60 shirts just to cover costs — only beyond that does she actually profit.
workingSteps: Identify the friend's mistake: confusing positive income with positive profit.
Reference the fixed cost (y-intercept of cost graph).
Reference the relative positions of the two graphs in the loss zone.

stimulus.inline: **Naledi's tutoring service** — R600 monthly rental + R30/student. Charges R150/student. Break-even at 5 students.

items.question: Naledi has 8 students in March. Calculate her profit.

stimulus.inline: **Naledi's tutoring service** — break-even at 5 students.

items.question: Naledi has only 3 students. Calculate her loss.

stimulus.inline: **Naledi's tutoring service** — break-even at 5 students.

items.question: Naledi is offered a marketing campaign for R200/month that she expects will bring her 2 more students. Is it worth it? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Yes. 2 extra students bring in 2 × R150 = R300 of income; the variable cost for them is 2 × R30 = R60; so extra contribution is R240/month. The campaign costs R200, leaving Naledi R40 better off per month. (She would need to lose only 1 student to fall to a marginal benefit, so the margin is thin — she should consider how reliable the prediction is.)
workingSteps: Calculate marginal income from 2 students: 2 × R150 = R300.
Calculate marginal variable cost: 2 × R30 = R60.
Net marginal benefit: R300 − R60 = R240/month.
Compare to campaign cost R200 → net gain R40.
Comment on risk: small margin, depends on actual uptake.

stimulus.inline: **Pretty's fudge stall** — R150 fixed weekly + R8 per batch. Sells at R20. Break-even: 13 batches / R260.

items.question: Pretty sells 25 batches one week. Calculate her profit.

stimulus.inline: **Pretty's fudge stall** — break-even at 13 batches.

items.question: Pretty wants to make at least R200 profit per week. How many batches must she sell?

stimulus.inline: **Zama's samoosa business** — R400 fixed + R3/samoosa, sells at R8. Break-even: 80 samoosas.

items.question: Zama sells 150 samoosas. Calculate her profit.

stimulus.inline: **Zama's samoosa business** — break-even at 80 samoosas.

items.question: Zama sells only 50 samoosas. State her zone and the loss amount.

stimulus.inline: **Zama's samoosa business** — break-even at 80 samoosas.

items.question: Zama is considering buying a bigger fryer for R1 000 (one-off cost). She thinks she can double output to 300 samoosas/month. Should she? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: At 300 samoosas: income = R2 400, cost = R400 + 300 × R3 = R1 300, profit = R1 100/month. At her current 150 samoosas (from previous question), profit was R350/month. The extra R750/month would cover the R1 000 fryer in under 2 months, so financially it's worth it — provided she actually achieves the higher output (demand might be the limit, not capacity).
workingSteps: Marginal benefit per month vs one-off cost.
Note risk: assumes demand follows capacity.

stimulus.inline: **Sandile's car wash** — R2 000 fixed + R15/car, R60/car. Break-even at 45 cars.

items.question: Sandile washes 60 cars in a month. Calculate his profit.

stimulus.inline: **Sandile's car wash** — break-even at 45 cars.

items.question: Sandile washes 80 cars. Compare his profit to the case of 60 cars and explain why doubling close to the break-even adds so much profit.
items.expectedAnswer: At 80 cars: income = R4 800, cost = R3 200, profit = R1 600. At 60 cars profit was R700. Going from 60 to 80 cars (a 33% increase in volume) more than doubles the profit (from R700 to R1 600). Once break-even is passed, every extra car contributes the full margin (price − variable cost = R60 − R15 = R45) directly to profit because the fixed cost is already covered.
workingSteps: Explain operating leverage: above break-even, every extra unit adds (price − variable cost) to profit.

stimulus.inline:
**Generic two-line graph picture**
A learner sees a cost graph and an income graph plotted on the same axes for a small business. The two lines cross at point P. Three labelled points A, B, C are marked: A is at x = 30 (income above cost), B is at x = 50 (the intersection), C is at x = 70 (cost above income).

items.question: Match each point to its zone.

stimulus.inline: **Generic business — cost graph y-intercept = R2 000, slope R10/unit. Income graph y-intercept = 0, slope R25/unit.**

items.question: Without computing the break-even point exactly, explain how each of these changes would affect the SIZE of the loss zone: (a) increase fixed cost, (b) increase price, (c) decrease variable cost.
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Higher fixed cost pushes the cost graph upward → loss zone gets bigger. (b) Higher price makes the income graph steeper → loss zone gets smaller. (c) Lower variable cost makes the cost graph flatter → loss zone gets smaller. The break-even point shifts left when income gets steeper or cost gets flatter, and right when fixed cost goes up.
workingSteps: Reason about y-intercept and slope changes to each graph.
Translate to break-even shift (left = smaller loss zone, right = larger).

stimulus.inline: **Themba's lemonade stand** — R50 fixed + R4/cup, sells at R10. Break-even at 9 cups.

items.question: Themba sells 20 cups. Calculate his profit.

stimulus.inline: **Themba's lemonade stand** — typically sells 20 cups/day for a R70 daily profit.

items.question: It rains for half the days in a week. On rainy days Themba sells only 5 cups. Calculate his weekly total profit/loss (7-day week, 4 sunny days at 20 cups, 3 rainy days at 5 cups).
workingSteps: Sunny days (4): each day profit R70 → 4 × R70 = R280 profit.
Rainy days (3): cost R50 + 5 × R4 = R70; income 5 × R10 = R50; loss = R20/day.
Weekly = R280 − R60 = R220 profit. Re-check: 4 sunny days × R70 = R280; 3 rainy × (-R20) = -R60; net = R220. NB tutor: verify answer key (expected R220 not R190).

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BREAKEVEN_ZONE: Identifies the wrong zone (profit vs loss) for a given volume
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BREAKEVEN_PROFIT_CONFUSE: Confuses break-even with the start of profit, or reports zero profit at break-even as 'profit'
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BREAKEVEN_INTERPRET: States the calculated number without translating it into business meaning
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BREAKEVEN_EQUATION: Sets up the break-even/profit equation incorrectly
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_GRAPH_INCOME_COST_SWAP: Confuses which graph is income vs cost
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_ROUNDING_CONTEXT: Reports a fractional answer when the context requires a whole number
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_SUBTRACTION_ORDER: Subtracts in the wrong order when computing profit / loss
